articles.title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
articles.summary: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
articles.body:
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for a long time.

Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.

Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.

And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Korçë and Vlora.

The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.

Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.

Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.

Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.

Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.

A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.

Every evening, throughout the summer for some 140 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.

The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.

The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.

One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.

Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania

'Flamingo Revolution' takes off as thousands demand Albanian PM's resignation

Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania

So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?

The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.

They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.

But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.

The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.

Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.

Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."

Another called Brunela said she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."

An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.

After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.

How is the government handling the unrest?

Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.

"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.

The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".

Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.

But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.

So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.

On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.

Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.

Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.

"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."

Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.

The UK government has urged visitors to check media for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.

Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

articles.title: Georgia renter warned his landlord about an 80-year-old tree next door after branches hit his home and truck; when it later crushed the house and left him paralysed, an appeals court revived his claims
articles.summary: A Georgia renter who suffered permanent paralysis when an ageing oak tree fell on his home has won a significant legal reprieve after an appeals court
articles.body: A Georgia renter who suffered permanent paralysis when an ageing oak tree fell on his home has won a significant legal reprieve after an appeals court revived his claims against his landlord. William Frank Jennings said he had repeatedly raised concerns about the tree, which stood on a neighbouring property but extended over the house he rented in Lindale, Georgia. According to the Georgia Court of Appeals ruling published on Justia on October 14, 2026, the trial court was wrong to dismiss his claims through summary judgment because factual questions remained about the landlord’s obligations and response to the reported danger. The decision allows the lawsuit to proceed, but does not establish liability.Repeated warnings about the ageing oak treeThe dispute began after Romulus Investments purchased a residential property at 10 Circle Drive in Lindale on April 2, 2021. Three days later, the company leased the house to Jennings for $650 a month. Next door, an empty lot at 8 Circle Drive contained an oak tree estimated to be more than 80 years old. Although its trunk stood on the neighbouring property, large limbs and branches stretched across the boundary and over Jennings’s rented house.According to the court record, branches fell on the house at least twice after Jennings moved in. In spring 2022, lightning struck the tree, sending another large limb onto his truck and damaging it. Jennings said he had told Christopher Alvey, one of Romulus Investments’ owners, that he believed the tree was decaying, dangerous, and needed inspection. He also said he had raised his concerns with other people at the landlord’s office when he visited to pay rent. According to the court’s account of the evidence, neither Romulus nor Carroll inspected the tree or took steps to address its overhanging branches. However, Alvey testified that Jennings had never notified him or Romulus about the danger. The appeals court said this conflict in the evidence raised a credibility issue that could not be resolved at the summary judgment stage.Tree collapse left tenant permanently paralysedOn July 14, 2022, the oak tree fell onto the rented house, crashing through the roof and trapping Jennings beneath the trunk and debris. Emergency responders arrived, but rescuers needed nearly two hours to free him from the destroyed building. The incident caused a severe spinal cord injury that left him permanently paralysed from the chest down. Jennings subsequently sued Romulus Investments and its two owners, Alvey and Wendell Rhodes, in the Superior Court of Floyd County. His claims included breach of the lease agreement, premises liability, failure to maintain the property in good repair and fit for habitation, and negligence under common law.He also sought compensatory damages, attorney fees and punitive damages. The landlord disputed the claims and sought summary judgment, arguing that the case could be resolved without a trial. The trial court granted that request. After an earlier appeal led to a remand for clarification of the ruling, the lower court again granted summary judgment, prompting Jennings to appeal once more.Why the appeals court revived the claimsThe Georgia Court of Appeals examined whether the landlord could have had a legal duty to respond to a hazard originating on neighbouring land. The lease required Romulus Investments to maintain the property and repair reported problems as soon as possible. It also instructed tenants to notify the landlord immediately about problems and to report known safety hazards. Georgia law also sets out landlords’ repair obligations and certain circumstances in which they may be liable for failing to repair leased premises. The Georgia Court of Appeals considered Sections 44-7-13 and 44-7-14 of the state code in assessing whether Jennings’s claims could proceed.The appellate judges said there was a genuine factual question about whether those obligations covered the danger posed by large branches repeatedly falling onto the rented property. They also rejected the lower court’s conclusion that an implied warranty of habitability could not apply because its express statutory codification took effect after the lease was signed. The court noted that Georgia law had recognised such a warranty before that codification.The judges further found that questions remained under Georgia’s premises-liability law and the statute governing a landlord’s responsibility for keeping leased premises in repair. The fact that the tree’s trunk stood on another property did not automatically resolve whether the landlord had a duty to address the hazard. The opinion also noted conflicting evidence over whether Jennings had notified the landlord, a credibility issue that could not be settled through summary judgment.What the ruling means for the lawsuitThe October 14 decision reversed the trial court’s summary judgment in favour of Romulus Investments and its owners. It also returned the questions of attorney fees and punitive damages to the lower court for further consideration. The ruling does not mean Jennings has won his negligence case or that the landlord has been found legally responsible for his injuries. Instead, it means his claims should not have been dismissed at this stage because material factual disputes remain.The case highlights the legal questions that can arise when a known hazard originates outside a rental property but threatens the safety of the home itself. The next stage will determine whether the evidence establishes liability and whether any damages are warranted.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Racism isn’t welcome’: Australian MP condemns anti-Indian stickers with ‘Remigration now’ message
articles.summary: Racist stickers targeting Indians have surfaced in Cessnock, a city in Australia's New South Wales state, featuring an image of a man of Indian appearance
articles.body: Racist stickers targeting Indians have surfaced in Cessnock, a city in Australia's New South Wales state, featuring an image of a man of Indian appearance defecating on a street and carrying the message, “Is this your culture? We don't like it!”The stickers also claim that 32 per cent of Australia's population is foreign-born, identify India as being at the top of the list and demand, “Remigration now!”David Repacholi, the federal MP for the area, condemned the material, describing the stickers as “disgusting racist” content and warning against attempts to spread hatred and division in the Hunter Region.“Racism isn't welcome in Cessnock. It isn't welcome in the Hunter. And it won't go unchallenged,” Repacholi wrote in a social media post.“Enough of this racist bullsh*t,” he added.Repacholi urged residents who come across the stickers to share their locations so they could be reported and removed. He also cautioned people against giving those responsible for the campaign more publicity than they deserved.This incident comes after similar stickers were reportedly found on Indian grocery products in supermarkets in July.The stickers reportedly featured a QR code directing people to the Fight for Australia campaign.She also shared printable sticker templates, telling followers they could print them at home or request copies by post.Similar incidents have reportedly been flagged in Brisbane, where stickers were found on Indian grocery products in local supermarkets.The incident comes months after anti-Indian leaflets were reportedly distributed in letterboxes across Kurri Kurri in the Hunter Region in July. articles.title: SC declines to interfere against HC reprieve to ex-min in Mahanga double murder case
articles.summary: Supreme Court dismisses SLP, upholds Orissa HC order quashing JMFC cognisance against ex-minister Pratap Jena in 2021 Mahanga double murder case.
articles.body: Cuttack: Supreme Court has dismissed a special leave petition (SLP) challenging an Orissa high court order which quashed the order of the court of judicial magistrate first class (JMFC), Salepur that had taken cognisance of offences against former BJD minister Pratap Jena as an accused in the Mahanga double murder case.The SLP was filed by Ranjit Kumar Baral, the younger son of BJP leader and chairman of Mahanga block, Kulamani Baral, who was killed, along with an associate, on Jan 2, 2021, while they were returning home on motorcycle.Initially, the double murder case was registered on a complaint filed by Ramakant Baral, the older son of Kulamani. Later after Ramakant’s death, Ranjit filed a fresh complaint. Ranjit had challenged the high court’s Oct 1, 2024, order.“We are not inclined to interfere with the impugned judgment/order of the high court,” SC’s two-judge bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh stated on Oct 15. Accordingly, the SLP is dismissed.The JMFC’s order, given on Sept 25, 2023, stated, “After going through the statements of the complainant, witnesses and other available materials on record, it found that a prima facie case punishable for the offences under Sections 302, 506, 120 B of the Indian Penal Code is made against the accused, Pratap Jena.”On Oct 1, 2025, the high court had stated that the JMFC’s order is not only unsustainable in the eye of law, but also the proceedings initiated against the petitioner (Pratap Jena) is absolutely without jurisdiction as his name was added as an additional accused who was not charge-sheeted even after two rounds of investigation and the court of sessions (trial court) had already assumed jurisdiction over the matter. “It was the court of sessions which could have passed the order to add the petitioner as an additional accused, but the sessions court had neither invoked its power nor was it moved to arraign the petitioner as an additional accused,” the high court said, adding, “In the interest of justice, the impugned order being unsustainable together with proceedings against the petitioner (Pratap Jena) is liable to be quashed.”On Aug 28, 2024, the court of additional sessions judge, Salepur, convicted nine of the accused in the Mahanga double murder case and awarded life imprisonment to them. articles.title: In 2012, a Michigan woman put her Troy home in her name and that of a woman who regarded her as a grandmother; 14 years later, an appeals court upheld the survivorship deed over her daughter's challenge
articles.summary: A Michigan appeals court has upheld a survivorship deed signed 14 years ago, ruling that a house in Troy belongs to a woman who was considered a
articles.body: A Michigan appeals court has upheld a survivorship deed signed 14 years ago, ruling that a house in Troy belongs to a woman who was considered a grandmother by the owner, rather than the owner's only legal heir. A three-judge panel of the Michigan Court of Appeals upheld a lower court decision that granted partial summary disposition in favour of Jessica Rae Harless. The legal challenge was brought by Anita Lanctot, who served as the personal representative of the estate of her late mother, Shirley Ann Page. The dispute focused on a single-family home at 212 Hickory Drive in Troy, Michigan. On 30 November 2012, Page signed and recorded a quitclaim deed that transferred the property from her sole ownership into the names of herself and Harless. Although Harless was not related to Page by blood or law, court records state that she considered Page her grandmother. After Page died on 12 September 2023, Lanctot filed a lawsuit in the Oakland Circuit Court to claim the property for her mother's estate.Challenge over property languageLanctot filed her civil lawsuit on 31 July 2024. Her claims included quiet title, deed reformation, statutory conversion, rescission, and identity theft. She argued that her mother's 2012 deed did not legally create a joint tenancy because it did not specifically use the word "joint" or "jointly". Under Michigan property law, when a property is transferred to two or more people, the law generally assumes they hold it as tenants in common rather than as joint tenants, unless the deed clearly states otherwise. Under a tenancy in common, a deceased owner's share passes to their heirs or estate. Under a joint tenancy with rights of survivorship, the property automatically passes to the surviving owner named in the deed. Lanctot argued that because the deed did not include the word "joint", it created only a tenancy in common. This would mean that Page's half of the property should pass to Lanctot as her mother's only legal heir. However, the main wording in Page's 2012 quitclaim deed stated that she transferred the house to herself and Harless "not as tenants in common, but with full rights of survivorship." On 6 June 2025, the Oakland Circuit Court granted partial summary disposition in favour of Harless on the quiet title and deed reformation claims. The judge ruled that clearly stating the right of survivorship was enough to create a joint tenancy with rights of survivorship. On 1 July 2025, the trial court transferred the remaining claims that did not concern ownership of the property to the district court and closed the circuit court case file. Lanctot then appealed the decision.Appeals court focus on grantor intentIn an unpublished opinion, the Michigan Court of Appeals rejected Lanctot's arguments and upheld the trial court's decision. The three-judge panel included Chief Judge Michael F. Gadola, Judge Colleen A. O'Brien, and Judge Philip P. Mariani. The court explained that Michigan law does not require specific words or phrases to create a joint tenancy. Instead, the main question is whether the person transferring the property clearly expressed an intention to give the surviving owner the right to keep it after their death. "The statute does not require any specific words to create a joint tenancy; however, the statute does require that the grantor's intent be clearly expressed in the instrument," the court stated in its ruling, citing section 554.44 of the Michigan Compiled Laws. The judges also addressed Lanctot's reliance on earlier court decisions, including the 1945 Michigan Supreme Court case Taylor v Taylor. They explained that earlier rulings focused on the property owner's intention, not simply on the exact words used. In Taylor, the Supreme Court ruled that using the word "jointly" in an opening paragraph did not automatically create a joint tenancy when the later paragraphs failed to make the owner's intention clear. The appeals court also referred to the 1925 Michigan Supreme Court case Kemp v Sutton. In that case, the state Supreme Court found that a testator had created a valid joint tenancy even though the document did not include what the court called the "talismanic words 'this is a joint tenancy.'"Plain meaning of the deedThe appeals court concluded that Page's choice of words made her intention for the home after her death clear. "Page used the terms 'not as tenants in common' and 'full rights of survivorship' in the deed, which, by their plain language, created a joint tenancy with rights of survivorship," the panel wrote. "If there was any uncertainty of intent when analyzing the deed language, the phrase 'not as tenants in common' clearly rebuts the presumption that the grantor intended to create a tenancy in common." The court found that the deed's wording was clear on its face. As a result, there was no genuine dispute over an important fact that would require a full trial or additional evidence. "The trial court did not need to go beyond the plain language of the deed to determine that Page's intent was to create a joint tenancy," the judges concluded. The ruling leaves Harless as the sole legal owner of the Troy home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A South Dakota couple built a 3,600-square-foot home for about $410,000 after living in a trailer for six years
articles.summary: Imagine living in a trailer for more than six years, then building a 3,600-square-foot family home with your own hands.
articles.body: Imagine living in a trailer for more than six years, then building a 3,600-square-foot family home with your own hands. That is exactly what Allison Brown and her husband did in South Dakota. They kept housing costs low, saved, and waited for the right moment to build. When contractor quotes proved too high, the couple became their own general contractors and finished the house for about $410,000. Their story offers practical lessons about patience, planning, family skills, and calculated risk. Read on to learn how a modest trailer helped fund a spacious dream home and an unexpected second income stream.Why a 1,500-square-foot trailer in South Dakota became the foundation for an affordable family homeIn 2019, Allison Brown and her husband bought a 1,500-square-foot trailer in a small South Dakota town. They believed it would be a permanent address. Brown told PEOPLE that they thought it would be their "forever home." Over the next six years, the family kept housing expenses low while raising their growing children. Brown, now 29, also said the trailer was the smartest financial choice available to them at the time. She explained that their combined monthly payment for everything was around $600, roughly half of the average rent or mortgage payment at that time. Low property taxes, favourable interest rates, and affordable prices before the pandemic helped, and she said a payment twice as high would have made saving impossible.How long commutes, a golf course community lot, and pricing fears shaped the decision to build in 2025The trailer was never meant to be a stepping stone, but life changed the plan. As Brown's children grew more involved in sports and other activities in a larger city about 25 to 30 minutes away, the drive took its toll. Around 2022, the couple found an affordable lot in a golf course community and decided the price was too attractive to ignore. Brown told PEOPLE that their manageable monthly housing costs were a major reason they could afford the purchase. Even so, they did not rush into construction. Watching building prices swing after the pandemic, she admitted she feared costs could skyrocket again. When prices levelled off toward the end of 2024 and into 2025, the couple decided to act and broke ground in April 2025.Self-building a 3,600-square-foot home for $410,000 against contractor quotes of $650,000 to $800,000When it was time to build, the couple chose to manage the project themselves instead of hiring a general contractor. PEOPLE reports that Brown's husband and her father-in-law both had years of hands-on construction experience. Although her husband never made a career of building, he knows everything about constructing a home, which she called a huge factor in making the project possible. Three contractors quoted between $650,000 and $800,000, yet the family finished the 3,600-square-foot house for about $410,000, saving an estimated $200,000 to $350,000. They price-matched every purchase and handled nearly all the work, including digging, rock hauling, siding, insulation, flooring, and masonry. She said that knowing the savings would reach hundreds of thousands made the decision easy.Basement space, better insulation, and storage: how trailer living shaped the design of the new homeLiving in the trailer taught the couple exactly what their next home needed. Brown told PEOPLE that the new house reflects everything she wished the trailer had offered. The design includes a basement where the children can spend time, better insulation to cope with South Dakota's harsh weather, and plenty of storage, all features the previous home lacked. For families considering a similar move, this approach is worth noting: years of daily life in a smaller space can reveal which features matter most and which are simply nice to have. Rather than guessing, the Browns built around real experience, turning past frustrations into specific design choices. The result is a 3,600-square-foot custom home that is the couple's dream house.Turning the trailer into an Airbnb rental and why the couple feels their building gamble paid offThe trailer did not disappear from the family's finances. Instead of selling it, the couple turned it into an Airbnb in their tourist-friendly hometown. Brown also told PEOPLE that managing the rental brings in more money than a regular full-time job would, and she described it as a major blessing. Looking back on the entire journey, she said it feels good to know how much money the family saved and that taking a huge risk has already placed them in a strong financial position. The couple now enjoys the home they built themselves while continuing to benefit from the decisions that made it possible. Their story suggests that affordable living, patience, practical skills, and a willingness to take calculated risks can combine into a stronger financial footing.You use AI every day.
